page: Microsoft Azure E16-8ds_v6 is a memory-optimized virtual machine featuring a constrained vCPU configuration. Built on the x86_64 architecture and running on Microsoft Hyper-V, this instance is powered by a 4.2 GHz Intel Xeon 8573C processor. It allocates 8 dedicated vCPUs spanning 4 physical cores with 2 threads per core, backed by 48 KB of L1d cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and a large 260 MB L3 cache. It incorporates advanced vector and matrix instructions, including AVX-512 and Intel AMX, but does not include hardware GPU acceleration.

The primary resource focus of the E16-8ds_v6 is its memory density, delivering 128.0 GB of RAM alongside 944 GB of high-speed local NVMe SSD storage. This yields an expansive memory ratio of 16.0 GB per vCPU. In benchmark testing, the instance exhibits strong single-core performance, achieving a Geekbench single-core score of 2154.0 and strong results in gzip single-threaded compression (31.38 GB/sec) and Geekbench text processing (2700.0). Cached memory bandwidth reaches 621.15 GB/sec, while large uncached block reads and writes register at 64.02 GB/sec and 43.34 GB/sec, respectively.

Multi-core compute and extended operations perform within the middle 50% benchmark tier, reflecting its constrained 8-vCPU allocation, with a multi-core Geekbench score of 8272.0 and PassMark CPU score of 14249.49. In database testing, the instance maintains steady throughput with 11.88 million Redis SET operations per second and a PassMark database operations score of 4990.18. For machine learning, small 135M model inference demonstrates strong generation speeds (276.83 tokens/sec), though larger 7B and 70B models exhibit weaker throughput due to CPU execution limits.

By constraining vCPUs to 8 while retaining the full 128 GB memory footprint and NVMe storage of a 16-vCPU tier, the E16-8ds_v6 provides substantial cost efficiency for software licensed per core. It is especially suited for in-memory databases, large cache layers, transactional relational databases, and data processing tasks requiring massive RAM and local scratch capacity without incurring redundant CPU licensing overhead.
